Orcasound · Salish Sea · 11 September 2026, 21:54 UTC

What the hydrophones actually heard

Every live Orcasound node over 9–9 September 2026, 1 calendar days and 3 node-days of audio, with a mechanical resonance at 4,816 Hz identified and rejected. It accounted for 113 of 758 detections.

8,176windows analysed
758detections with audio
113rejected as resonance
645detections remaining

What was run

3 hydrophones, Bush Point, North San Juan Channel, Lab, over 9–9 September 2026, 1 calendar days and 3 node-days of audio: 8,176 thirty-second windows, 68 hours of audio. OrcaHello, a Southern Resident presence detector, flagged 758 of them as holding at least one positive segment, which is 9.3% of the audio. Every one was measured for the resonance. None was classified for ecotype: this is an unreviewed sample of model candidates, ranked by OrcaHello's whole-window confidence.

  • Bush Point · Admiralty Inlet, off Whidbey Island · 48.03°N, 122.61°W · 24 h over 1 days
  • Lab · Haro Strait, west side of San Juan Island · 48.56°N, 123.17°W · 23 h over 1 days
  • North San Juan Channel · north San Juan Channel · 48.62°N, 123.09°W · 21 h over 1 days

Two counts exist and they are not the same. OrcaHello also returns a whole-window verdict, which fires on 499 windows; 259 further windows hold a positive segment without it. This page counts segments throughout, because a segment is what produces a clip to listen to.

Not included, because they are inactive in the feed registry rather than quietly missing:

  • Orcasound MaST Center · node offline upstream; acoustic signal stopped 2026-07-12, segments continued until 2026-07-17
  • Orcasound Point Robinson · hydrophone sediment-buried; the node streams but carries no usable signal

The 4,816 Hz resonance

Frozen Perch 2.0 embeddings put Bush Point's saturated hours in a single tight non-biological cluster, 26.3 standard deviations tighter than true background, that no other hydrophone contributed a detection to. That said the audio was not whales. It did not say what it was.

It is a high-Q mechanical resonance: a fundamental at 4,816 Hz, 20.5 dB over true background, −3 dB width 62 Hz so Q = 78, carrying integer overtones at 2× and 3× and nothing at 0.5×. Across two days its centre holds to a standard deviation of 87 Hz, 1.8%. It is struck rather than running: 15.5 dB in windows the detector fired on against 1.4 dB in windows it did not. That is a metal object near the hydrophone, moved by water, ringing at its fundamental mode.

The spectrum below is not a single line at 4,816 Hz, and the claim does not need it to be. There is further raised structure between roughly 5 and 7 kHz, one part of it higher than either marked overtone. Struck plates and bars ring in inharmonic modes as well as integer ones, so extra peaks are what a metal object should look like rather than a problem for the reading. What carries the identification is the narrowness of the 4,816 Hz peak (Q = 78), the stability of its centre across days, its integer overtones, and the absent subharmonic, not its being the only feature in the band.

A Southern Resident call is tonal with a harmonic stack in roughly 1–6 kHz, and so is this, which is why spectral flatness, centroid, band ratios and pairwise spectrum similarity all failed to separate it. The sound is not un-whale-like in its spectrum. It simply never changes, and none of those measures were measuring change.

Before and after

The threshold is calibrated on this sample: 18 dB sits about 1.3 dB above the highest tone measured at the nodes where the object is absent. It is a filter for one object at one hydrophone, not a general de-noiser, and another site's contaminant will sit somewhere else in the spectrum.

Whether the numbers can be trusted

These are model candidates and nothing more. OrcaHello's confidence orders windows for listening. It is not a probability that a whale is present, it is not calibrated per hydrophone, and no false-positive floor has been applied to it.

Removing the resonance does not make what remains whales. It removes one identified contaminant. Nothing on this page has been reviewed or classified to ecotype.

Does what survives hold up?

No embedding test was supplied, so the detections remaining after the filter have not been independently checked.

What survives, and what it sounds like

13 clips, drawn from detections that survived the filter, strongest OrcaHello whole-window confidence first within each site and spread across days so one busy hour cannot fill the sample. No ecotype was assessed, so no card makes a species claim beyond the detector's own. This is a listening sample and not a census. 13 of 13 clips are the full call bout rebuilt from the 30s source window.

Limitations

  • OrcaHello gates everything on this page. 9.3% of this audio was flagged at all, and a Bigg's call has to sound Southern-Resident enough to trip a Southern-Resident detector.
  • The cards are ranked by OrcaHello's whole-window confidence, which is uncalibrated. A high score is a reason to listen first, not evidence of a whale.
  • The rejection threshold is one number, set from earlier tone measurements at three nodes with roughly 1.3 dB of margin. It is a filter for one object at one hydrophone.
  • No ecotype classifier ran, so nothing here separates Southern Residents, Bigg's and humpbacks.
  • These are the three live Orcasound nodes. MaST Center and Point Robinson are dead upstream and are listed above rather than omitted.
